this is the only time we discuss eastman house and id like this section to at least touch on this incredible building and how unique it is in teh way it is built like a factory and how it reflects on how practical eastman was. see this note from gemini ==Yes, behind its elegant mansion exterior, the [George Eastman House](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=/m/09rdzl) was built exactly like a fireproof factory==. [1, 2]

Because George Eastman worked constantly with highly unstable, flammable photographic chemicals and cellulose nitrate films, he was utterly obsessed with fire safety. While the outside was designed in a beautiful Georgian Revival style, the actual structural core relied on industrial factory engineering. [1, 2, 3]

## Industrial Structural Features

- Reinforced Concrete & Steel: The entire frame of the 50-room mansion is constructed from steel-reinforced concrete rather than standard residential wood framing. [1, 2]
- Thick Outer Walls: The exterior walls are 14 inches thick, utilizing heavy Roman brick and limestone accents. [1, 3]
- Concrete Roof: Unlike typical homes of the era with wooden roof trusses, the mansion features a solid concrete roof deck. [1]
- Sliding Steel Doors: Heavy, industrial-grade steel doors were hidden in the walls and could be slid shut to instantly isolate rooms and contain fires. [1]

## Advanced State-of-the-Art Utilities

To match its industrial durability, Eastman packed the house with commercial-grade technologies that were incredibly rare for a 1905 home: [4]

- Private Power Plant: The estate operated its own independent electrical generator.
- Central Vacuum System: A built-in, centralized vacuum network ran through the walls of the entire mansion.
- Massive Communications Network: The house featured a central clock network and an internal telephone system boasting 21 active stations. [1, 2, 4]

notes.text:
▎ The house itself was the truest thing he ever built about himself. From the street it was a Georgian Revival mansion on East Avenue; underneath, it was a factory, because he had spent his life around nitrate film and chemistry that liked to burn. The frame was steel-reinforced concrete, the walls and even the floors were fourteen inches thick, the roof was concrete, and steel doors could slide shut to seal off a burning room. It had its own power house, reached by tunnel, an internal telephone exchange with twenty-one stations, a vacuum system built into the walls, a master clock keeping every room on the same minute, and a dairy in the basement fed by his own cows out back. Other men's fortunes built palaces for display. His built a factory wearing a mansion's clothes.
▎
▎ And he ran it like one. In 1919, when the conservatory's square proportions would not stop bothering him, he did not redecorate. (needs to read as acoustics being what drove this - it's not clear here) He had the house cut in two and the entire rear half, twenty-five hundred tons of it, jacked nine feet four inches along rails until the room was right, for more than twice what the whole house had cost to build. Every morning an organist arrived, at seven in summer and seven-thirty in winter, to play him through breakfast while he did business. In that house even beauty ran on a schedule, and when it drifted out of spec, it got re-engineered.
